speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Good morning, David. Thanks for making time. I'm Priya, I'll be the lead consultant on your GreenBuild engagement. Before we dive in, can you give me a quick picture of Meridian Manufacturing's operations?

speaker: David Park
text: Morning Priya. Sure. Meridian makes automotive components — mostly brake assemblies and suspension parts. We have three plants, two in Ohio and one in Tennessee. About 1,200 employees across all sites. Annual revenue is around 340 million.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Got it. And what's driving the carbon reporting initiative? Is this regulatory, customer-driven, or internal commitment?

speaker: David Park
text: Honestly, it's all three. Two of our biggest customers, Ford and Stellantis, are now requiring Scope 3 supplier emissions data as part of their procurement process. We're also above the SEC reporting threshold, so we'll need to file starting next year. And our board just adopted a sustainability charter.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: That's a strong set of drivers. The good news is our standard engagement covers exactly what you need for the SEC filing — Scope 1 and 2 plus selected Scope 3 categories. And the supplier data your OEM customers are asking for falls under Scope 1 and 2 from your perspective, since it's your direct emissions.

speaker: David Park
text: Right. So how exactly does the process work? We've never done a formal carbon inventory before.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: We follow the GHG Protocol Corporate Standard, which is the framework the SEC and most global regulators recognize. There are four phases — discovery, data collection, analysis, and reporting. Total timeline is typically ten to thirteen weeks for a manufacturer your size.

speaker: David Park
text: Thirteen weeks is tight. We need to have numbers ready for our board meeting in August. Is that doable if we start in April?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: April start, August deadline gives us about eighteen weeks. That's comfortable even with buffer for data collection delays, which are common with first-time engagements. We should be fine.

speaker: David Park
text: What kind of data will you need from us? I want to make sure we have the right people lined up to pull it.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: The biggest items are utility bills for the past 24 months — natural gas and electricity for all three plants. Then fleet fuel records, production output logs so we can calculate intensity metrics, and refrigerant purchase records from your HVAC maintenance.

speaker: David Park
text: Utility bills and production logs we have. The refrigerant records might be scattered — our maintenance team uses different systems at each plant. Is that a problem?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Not uncommon. We'll work with your maintenance team to reconstruct the data from purchase orders and service logs. Refrigerant leaks are often a surprisingly large emissions source in manufacturing — we've seen cases where a single facility's refrigerant leaks are equivalent to 30 or 40 tonnes of CO2.

speaker: David Park
text: Really? That's more than I would have guessed. What about our supply chain emissions? Ford specifically asked about our upstream footprint.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: That's Scope 3. Our standard engagement covers Category 1 — purchased goods and services — plus upstream transportation and waste. Those are the most material categories for manufacturers. We'd survey your top suppliers for primary data and use industry averages for the rest.

speaker: David Park
text: How many suppliers would you need to survey? We have over 200 active suppliers.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: We typically focus on the top 30 to 50 by spend. They usually represent 70 to 80 percent of your procurement emissions. The rest we estimate using spend-based emission factors from databases like EEIO.

speaker: David Park
text: Okay. Now, we export brake assemblies to our Stellantis plant in Germany. I've been hearing about something called CBAM — a carbon border tax. Does that affect us?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: CBAM currently covers cement, steel, aluminum, fertilizers, electricity, and hydrogen. Auto parts aren't directly covered yet, but if your assemblies contain steel or aluminum components, your EU customers may need to report the embedded emissions in those materials. We can do a CBAM assessment as an add-on.

speaker: David Park
text: Our brake assemblies are about 60% steel by weight. So yes, that's relevant. How much does the CBAM add-on cost?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: It's fifteen thousand per product line. For your brake assemblies and suspension parts, that would be two product lines, so thirty thousand. It calculates the embedded carbon per unit so your EU customers can report accurately.

speaker: David Park
text: I'll need to discuss that with our CFO. What about carbon offsets? If our numbers come back high, can we purchase offsets to bring them down for reporting purposes?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: That's a good question. Offsets are, well, it's a complicated area. The market is evolving. We generally recommend focusing on actual emission reductions first before looking at offsets. The reporting frameworks tend to distinguish between actual reductions and offset credits.

speaker: David Park
text: But can you help us evaluate offset options? Like, do you have partnerships with offset providers? Our board specifically asked about this.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: We can certainly discuss it as part of the reduction roadmap phase. Let me look into what our current offering is on the offset advisory side and get back to you. I don't want to give you incomplete information.

speaker: David Park
text: Fair enough. Switching topics — what does the assurance piece look like? The SEC requires third-party assurance, right?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Correct. The SEC requires limited assurance initially, moving to reasonable assurance by 2033. GreenBuild isn't an assurance provider ourselves — we prepare the data and documentation, then an independent auditor like Deloitte or EY verifies it. We have an assurance readiness add-on that prepares you for that audit.

speaker: David Park
text: What's the cost of the assurance readiness add-on?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Eighteen thousand dollars. It includes documentation formatting, evidence packaging, and a pre-audit walkthrough. Most clients find it saves significant time and back-and-forth during the actual audit.

speaker: David Park
text: Let's include that. And the base engagement — for three facilities with Scope 1, 2, and the Scope 3 categories you mentioned — what's the total investment?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: For three manufacturing facilities, standard engagement, I'd estimate 65 to 75 thousand. Plus the assurance readiness at 18 thousand. And if you decide on the CBAM assessment, that's another 30 thousand. So the range is 83 thousand on the low end to 123 thousand with everything.

speaker: David Park
text: That's within the range our CFO approved. Let me confirm the CBAM piece after I speak with the EU sales team. Can you send a formal proposal with those numbers?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Absolutely. I'll have a proposal to you by Friday with the breakdown, timeline, and team assignments. I'll include a data request list so your team can start gathering utility bills and production records in the meantime.

speaker: David Park
text: Perfect. One last question — who on your side will be doing the actual analysis work?

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: I'll be the engagement lead. You'll also work with our data analyst, Kenji Nakamura, who specializes in manufacturing sector emissions. And our regulatory specialist, Anna Reyes, will handle the SEC filing format and assurance preparation. I'll include their bios in the proposal.

speaker: David Park
text: Sounds good. Looking forward to the proposal on Friday. Thanks Priya.

speaker: Priya Sharma
text: Thank you David. We'll get this done well before your August board meeting. Talk soon.
